rationale: A wins because it knows what not to pitch. Its refusal of "Glossier expands its fragrance line with three new launches" is exactly the adult move: the update gives no scent, price, perfumer, or category data, so it keeps the weak product news out of the main set. B walks straight into that hole with "A brand born from a beauty blog is now betting on the perfume aisle," then props it up with an invented category trend. That is how a mediocre pitch gets dressed for a party and still can't get past the door.
gaps_in_A: "The beauty blog that became a brand is now a shelf-space negotiation" is a strong feature frame, but it leans on "one of the few brands with a clean twelve-year arc" without proof from the update.
"Sephora is betting more shelf on a brand whose numbers nobody outside can see" is useful, but "Sephora and LVMH's specialty-retail strategy" imports ownership/context not supplied in the fact block.
"suburban strip-mall retail rather than mall-and-city Sephora" overstates what "Sephora at Kohl's" proves. Good instinct, but it needs confirmation before it becomes copy.
gaps_in_B: "covering the collapse of the direct-to-consumer thesis" is too grand for one Glossier announcement. The update supports a Glossier reversal, not an obituary for DTC.
"A brand born from a beauty blog is now betting on the perfume aisle" turns three unnamed fragrance products into a category bet. That is a product-launch fact wearing a trend coat.
"covering the wave of beauty brands extending into scent" is invented context. If the wave matters, bring outside evidence; don't conjure it because the sentence wants lift.
"is there any evidence fragrance performs better on a physical shelf than DTC?" is the right question, but it should have killed the fragrance angle, not appeared after the set already pitched it.
